newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - DEC CPI UP, MONEY SUPPLY EASING.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - DEC CPI UP, MONEY SUPPLY EASING.

text.p: South African consumer price inflation will have increased again in December 1996 to the highest level since June 1995, mainly as a result of a one point hike in mortgage interest rates, analysts said.

The consensus forecast of economists polled by Reuters was for a year-on-year inflation rate of 9.6 percent from 9.2 percent in November, and a month-on-month increase of 1.0 percent compared to 0.4 percent.
The data is due for release at 0900 GMT on Tuesday.

"The bulk of the monthly increase will come from the Bank rate move which will come into the December number by pushing up the mortgage rate," said Michael McClintock, economist at SBC Warburg in Johannesburg.
The Reserve Bank announced a surprise one percentage point increase in Bank rate to 17 percent in late November, triggering a similar increase in home loan rates to 20 percent.
Other contributors to higher inflation in December include increased fuel costs, high meat prices over the Christmas period and a quarterly review of furniture prices, economists said.

The full effects of the rand's fall of over a fifth against a basket of currencies in 1996 have yet to feed fully through the system and analysts predict inflation will continue to trend higher in the early part of 1997.
Nick Barnardt, economist at BOE NatWest, said he expected CPI to peak at 10.8 percent in May.
But the average for the current year was expected to be under 10 percent, according to most economists and government officials.
Also due next Tuesday at 1500 GMT are preliminary data for December M3 money supply and private sector credit extension growth.

Analysts expect both figures to come down, mainly as a result of the very high year-ago comparative base. The consensus forecast was for M3 year-on-year growth of 14.3 percent from 15.32 in November while private credit is seen expanding 16.3 percent against 17.10 percent.

There was talk in the market that the November credit figure might be revised up due to a miscalculation by one major bank, but banking sources said on Friday they were unaware of any revised figures being submitted to the central bank.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said earlier this week he remained concerned about excessive money supply and credit growth. He told Reuters he was happy to see the daily money market shortage stay above 10 billion rand since this discouraged bank lending.
The 1996 guideline for M3 growth is six to 10 percent. The Bank has yet to set 1997 guidelines.

Dawie Roodt, economist at Equisec, said the growth in the monetary aggregates should start to slow sharply in the early months of 1997 as November's interest rate hike chokes off credit demand in an economy which is already slowing markedly.
Roodt said he saw scope for a cut in official interest rates as early as the first quarter, although most other economists are betting Stals will hold his hand until around mid-year.
Internationally, Europe will take a back seat in the coming week, as economic releases from the U.S. and Japan provide the major focus for investors, analysts said.

After recent data releases tossed the U.S. market to and fro, the countdown to the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting (FOMC) in early February will start with key employment and gross domestic product data.
"Most of the data we've had recently has been fairly knife- edge stuff," said Andy Cossor, fixed income analyst at Technical Data in London.
"The employment cost index (ECI) will give a guide to inflation, and combined with the guide to growth from fourth quarter GDP should set the tone for the FOMC the week after."
The U.S. will release the fourth quarter ECI on Tuesday. Fourth quarter GDP was scheduled for release on Friday. Analysts said investors were still concerned about wage pressures.

"The ECI is one of the more reliable indicators," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston in London. "Everyone is now priced for strong GDP numbers, but the ECI seems to be better behaved than wages."
Japan faces a data overload. Industrial production and retail sales were due on Wednesday, and consumer prices, unemployment, construction orders and housing starts on Friday.
